title: FBI Probes $300 Million in Argentina Football Contracts After World Cup Final Drama
excerpt: U.S. authorities are investigating more than $300 million in commercial contracts linked to the Argentine Football Association, with FBI agents reportedly questioning officials at JFK Airport moments after the World Cup final.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • FBI questioned AFA officials at JFK Airport after Argentina's World Cup final loss.
  • U.S. probes over $300 million in AFA contracts for potential money laundering.
  • AFA denies claims of summoned officials but acknowledges a third party was subpoenaed.
  • Investigation follows December raids in Argentina targeting football finances.

FBI agents questioned the president and treasurer of Argentina's Football Association at New York's JFK International Airport on Monday morning, just hours after the national team's 1-0 loss to Spain in the 2026 World Cup final, according to Argentine media outlet Infobae.

AFA president Claudio "Chiqui" Tapia and treasurer Pablo Toviggino were reportedly approached by federal agents aboard a bus on the airport tarmac as the Argentine delegation prepared to board a charter flight to Buenos Aires. The questioning lasted approximately 30 minutes, according to a witness cited by Reuters, delaying the flight's departure from its scheduled 6:00 a.m. time to around 8:15 a.m.

What the FBI Is Investigating

U.S. prosecutors are examining whether more than $300 million in commercial contracts linked to the AFA were used to funnel money through American banks, according to Infobae. The investigation centers on potential money laundering and fraud involving sponsorship deals and commercial partnerships.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=8lO72XZsAr8

A key focus of the probe is Tourprodenter, a Florida-based organization that handled payments related to some of Argentina's largest commercial deals, according to GiveMeSport. Court documents reportedly indicate that Tapia may be asked to provide information about the entity's operations.

Investigators are also examining the roles of businessmen Diego Lucero and Javier Faroni, who are allegedly under investigation for fraud and embezzlement alongside Tapia and Toviggino, according to multiple reports citing Infobae.

AFA's Forceful Denial

The AFA pushed back hard against the reports on Wednesday, releasing a detailed statement calling the claims "completely untrue."

https://www.instagram.com/p/DbBcsJmgFgq/

"It is absolutely false to claim that Claudio Tapia or Pablo Toviggino have been summoned to testify by the United States justice system. It is also false to claim that their cell phones or any other electronic devices have been seized."

— Argentine Football Association statement

The association acknowledged, however, that a third party — whose identity the AFA did not disclose — had been summoned to appear before a U.S. grand jury and potentially provide evidence about several people, including AFA officials. The statement stressed that "the document in question does not impose any personal measure on the President of the AFA or its Treasurer, does not order their appearance, does not impose any procedural obligation on them."

Previous Raids in December
Based on reports from Infobae and Reuters.

The airport incident is part of wider scrutiny of Argentine football finances. Reuters reported that the current U.S. investigation follows raids conducted in Argentina in December as part of a broader money-laundering probe targeting the country's football establishment.

https://x.com/PolymarketFC/status/2080013966118392247

The case echoes the landmark 2015 FIFA corruption scandal, when U.S. prosecutors charged dozens of football officials from across the Americas with racketeering, wire fraud, and money laundering. That investigation, also run out of federal courts in New York, reshaped global football governance and led to the downfall of several South American football federation leaders.

What Comes Next

According to court documents cited by The Sun, Tapia is expected to appear before the Southern District Court of Florida in connection with the investigation. The scope of any potential charges — or whether the probe will expand to additional officials — remains unclear.

The timing adds another layer of crisis for the AFA. Argentina's delegation was already reeling from the World Cup final loss to Spain at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, and FIFA has separately launched a disciplinary investigation into post-final clashes involving Argentine players and coaching staff.

AFA's Response to Allegations
›AFA denies claims of officials being summoned.
›Claims of device seizures are labeled false.
›Acknowledges a third party was subpoenaed.
›Stresses no personal measures against Tapia or Toviggino.
AFA statement.

For the millions of Argentine football fans worldwide — including a sizable diaspora in the United States — the allegations threaten to overshadow the team's on-field legacy. The investigation's U.S. nexus, with its focus on money flowing through American banks and a Florida-based intermediary, means the case will unfold in jurisdictions with aggressive financial crime enforcement, potentially with consequences that extend well beyond Argentine football.
image_caption: Claudio Tapia, president of the Argentine Football Association, photographed in 2020. Tapia was reportedly questioned by FBI agents at JFK Airport following the 2026 World Cup final.
nri_angle: The investigation's focus on money flowing through U.S. banks could have implications for Argentine football operations in the United States, home to one of the largest Argentine diaspora communities.
